title: Hard Questions
subtitle: Honest answers for a skeptical age
blurb: Essays answering the questions people actually ask, suffering and evil, hell, miracles, science, the reliability of the Bible, the hiddenness of God, and whether faith is reasonable at all.

chapters.title: Can a Reasonable Person Believe in Miracles?
chapters.summary: Modern people are taught that miracles are the one thing an educated person cannot accept, and that confidence rests on an argument worth examining.
chapters.body:
There is a feeling, deep in the modern mind, that the question of miracles was settled long ago, that science closed the door and grown-ups walked through it. People do not rise from the dead. Water does not turn to wine. We know how the world works now, and the world does not work like that. To believe otherwise is to believe in a flat earth, a charming relic from before we knew better. This feeling is so widespread that it usually does not present itself as an argument at all. It presents itself as maturity.

But there is a real argument underneath the feeling, and it is worth stating at full strength, because it is a good one. The philosopher David Hume gave it its classic form in the eighteenth century, and it still does most of the work even for people who have never read him. A miracle, Hume said, is a violation of the laws of nature. The laws of nature are established by the most uniform and constant experience there is, billions of observations with no exception. The evidence for any reported miracle, by contrast, is some human testimony, and human testimony is notoriously unreliable, full of error, exaggeration, wishful thinking, and lies. So whenever you weigh a miracle report, you are weighing the most solid evidence imaginable, the uniform laws of nature, against the flimsiest, a few people's say-so. The wise man, Hume concluded, proportions his belief to the evidence, and the evidence will always favor the natural explanation. It is always more likely that the witnesses were mistaken than that the dead rose.

Notice how much of this is right, because it is mostly right. Human testimony is unreliable. People do exaggerate and deceive and see what they want to see. Most miracle reports, examined closely, do dissolve into rumor or fraud or honest mistake, and a healthy skepticism toward them is not arrogance but good sense. If a man tells you his uncle came back from the dead last Tuesday, you are right to doubt him, and you would be foolish to do otherwise. Hume is correct that extraordinary claims call for proportionate scrutiny. The error is not in the caution. The error is somewhere more subtle.

Here is the first crack. Hume's argument quietly defines the laws of nature as having no exceptions, and then uses that definition to rule out any reported exception in advance. But that is reasoning in a circle. The whole question is whether an exception has ever occurred. If you build the impossibility of exceptions into your definition of the laws, you have not discovered that miracles do not happen. You have assumed it before looking. The laws of nature describe what happens when nature is left to itself. They are descriptions of the regular pattern, the default behavior of matter. They are not laws in the sense of legislation that forbids anything. The law that dropped objects fall does not forbid me from catching a falling cup. My hand is not a violation of gravity. It is a new factor introduced into the situation. The question of miracles is exactly whether there is anyone outside the system who can introduce a new factor, the way my hand interrupts the fall of the cup without breaking any law of physics.

This is where the whole debate turns, and it turns on something that comes before the evidence. Whether miracles are possible depends entirely on whether God exists. If there is no God, if the physical universe is all there is and it runs as a closed system, then of course there are no miracles, because there is no one outside the machine to reach in. But if there is a God who made the regularities in the first place, then the regularities are not a cage that binds Him. They are His ordinary way of working, and there is no reason in principle He could not, on rare and meaningful occasions, do something else. The author of a story is bound by its rules only as long as he chooses to be. So the real question is never simply is this miracle report credible in isolation. It is also is there a God who might act, and what you already believe about that determines how you will read every report before you read it.

There is a further weakness in Hume's argument that later thinkers pressed hard, and it is worth seeing because it shows the reasoning proves too much. Hume says we should always reject the miracle because uniform experience stands against it. But uniform experience is exactly what is in dispute. To say experience is uniformly against miracles, you would have to know in advance that every reported miracle in history was false, which is the very thing you are trying to establish. You cannot use the claim no miracle has ever happened as evidence that this particular miracle did not happen, because the first claim is just the conclusion stated early. And there is a stranger problem. By Hume's logic, you should reject any sufficiently unprecedented event, no matter how good the testimony, simply because it is unprecedented. But science advances precisely by accepting well-attested events that overturn what uniform experience had suggested. If researchers had reasoned like Hume, they would have rejected every anomaly that did not fit the existing pattern, and the anomalies are often where the truth was hiding. A method that forbids you ever to believe the genuinely new is not a method for finding truth. It is a method for protecting what you already think.

This exposes something uncomfortable about the confident modern dismissal. It often presents itself as following the evidence, but it is frequently doing the reverse. It begins with the assumption that the universe is a closed system, that nothing outside nature exists or acts, and then it concludes that miracles cannot happen. But that assumption, philosophical naturalism, is not a discovery of science. Science studies the regular workings of nature, which is exactly what it should do, and it has nothing to say about whether anything exists beyond nature. The leap from science describes the regular pattern to nothing ever breaks the pattern is a philosophical leap, not a scientific finding, and it is usually made without notice. The person who says a reasonable man cannot believe in miracles has often smuggled in the conclusion at the start.

Now take the case the whole question really hangs on, because Christianity does not ask you to believe in miracles in general. It asks you to believe in one in particular, on which it stakes everything. Paul wrote that if Christ has not been raised, the entire faith is worthless and Christians are to be pitied. He did not hedge. He bet the farm on a historical event. So examine that one. What actually has to be explained is a cluster of facts that even most skeptical historians grant. A man named Jesus was crucified under Pontius Pilate and died. His followers, devastated and scattered, within a few weeks were proclaiming in the very city where he was killed that they had seen him alive. They went from terrified hiders to public witnesses who would not stop talking even under threat of death. The movement exploded out of Jerusalem, where anyone could have produced the body and ended it in an afternoon, and no one did. Within a generation there were written accounts naming witnesses still alive.

The naturalist has to explain those facts without a resurrection, and he can try. Maybe they stole the body and lied. But people do not die for what they know to be a lie, and these people died for this. Maybe they hallucinated. But hallucinations are private, and the reports describe groups, meals, conversations, a man eating fish. Maybe the legend grew over centuries. But the core proclamation is too early for that, traceable to within a few years of the event, far too soon for myth to crystallize while eyewitnesses were still around to object. Each natural explanation has been offered, and each has serious trouble, and the honest historian, even the unbelieving one, usually ends by saying we know the early Christians sincerely believed they had seen him risen, and there it stops, because the historian as historian cannot say what caused the belief. N.T. Wright has argued at book length that the rise of the resurrection belief is itself a fact in need of explanation, and that no first-century Jew would have invented a single risen messiah out of thin air, because it fit nothing they expected. Something happened. The question is what.

This is the point. Belief in the resurrection is not a flight from evidence. It is one explanation among several for a real body of historical data, and it is not obviously the worst one. It looks impossible only if you have already decided, before examining anything, that the universe is closed and God cannot act. If you have decided that, then no evidence could ever be enough, because any natural explanation, however strained, will always beat a miracle by definition, which is exactly Hume's circle running again. But if you hold the question open, if you grant that there might be a God who could act, then the resurrection stops being absurd and becomes a hypothesis you weigh like any other, against the alternatives, on the evidence.

It is worth being honest about what does and does not follow, because Christians sometimes oversell this. The historical case does not prove the resurrection the way a syllogism proves its conclusion. History does not deal in proof of that kind. What the historical case does is shift the burden. It establishes a body of facts, the death, the empty tomb, the transformed witnesses, the sudden explosion of a movement proclaiming a risen and crucified messiah in the teeth of every expectation, that demand some explanation. It then shows that the natural explanations on offer are strained, each one buying its naturalism at the price of ignoring part of the data. At that point the resurrection is no longer the desperate option. It is a live one, sitting on the table next to the others, and the only thing that automatically rules it out is the prior assumption that nothing outside nature can act. Strip that assumption away, hold the question genuinely open, and a thoughtful person can look at the evidence and conclude that the best explanation is the one the witnesses gave, that he was raised. That is not blind faith. That is following the evidence past the point where a closed mind had decided in advance it was not allowed to go.

So I will not tell you that you must believe Jesus rose. That is a larger step and it involves more than argument. What I will tell you is that the confident claim that a reasonable person simply cannot believe such a thing does not survive examination. It rests on a definition that assumes its own conclusion and on a philosophy of nature that pretends to be a finding of science when it is not. A reasonable person can certainly reject miracles. But he cannot do it on the cheap, by waving the word science and assuming the door is closed. The door is exactly what is in question. Whether anyone is on the other side of it is the oldest question there is, and it is still open, and the empty tomb is still sitting there, in the historical record, waiting for an explanation that you have not yet been given a reason to refuse.

chapters.title: Can You Actually Trust the Bible?
chapters.summary: You have heard that the Bible was copied, changed, and voted on by men with an agenda, so here is what the evidence actually shows.
chapters.body:
Somebody has probably said it to you already, maybe in a comment section, maybe across a lunch table. The Bible has been copied and recopied and translated so many times that whatever Jesus actually said is long gone, like a game of telephone stretched across two thousand years. By the time it reached you, it is a copy of a copy of a copy of a translation of a forgery. And on top of that, some powerful church officials sat in a room centuries later and voted on which books got in and which got burned, conveniently picking the ones that kept them in charge. So why would you ever hand a book like that your actual life.

That is a fair thing to feel, and I am not going to scold you for feeling it. I want to give you the objection at full strength before I answer it, because you deserve the real version, not a strawman I can knock over with one finger.

Here is the strongest form. We do not possess a single original document. Not one. Every Bible you have ever held is a translation of copies of copies, and the people doing the copying were human, which means they made mistakes, and at least some of them had reasons to shade things in their own direction. On top of that, the books themselves were written decades after the events by people who already believed, so they are not neutral reporters, they are fans writing about their hero. And then the canon, the official list of which books count, was settled by church councils that had real political power on the line, which means the Bible is not a book that floated down from heaven. It is a committee product. So the whole thing could be unreliable all the way down at the foundation, and you would have no way of knowing.

Now let me walk through it slowly, because almost every single piece of that objection has a real answer, and the answers turn out to be more interesting than the objection itself.

Start with the telephone problem, because it is the one that sounds most devastating and gets repeated the most. Telephone works as an insult because in the actual game there is only one chain. One person whispers to the next, the message degrades down a single line, and there is no way to check it against anything. But that is simply not how the New Testament was copied. By the second and third centuries, copies were being made in many different places at the same time, in different languages, by communities that did not all know one another and frequently disagreed with one another about important things. So instead of one fragile chain, you get a giant family tree spreading out in every direction across the ancient world. And here is why that completely changes the picture. When you have thousands of copies made independently in scattered places, you can compare them against each other and spot exactly where a scribe slipped, the same way you can catch a typo in your own essay by comparing several drafts. An error introduced by a tired scribe in Egypt does not show up in the copies made in Syria or Rome, so it stands out as the odd one and you can see it for what it is. We are not stuck guessing what got changed. We can reconstruct it.

And the sheer amount of material is the thing that genuinely surprised me when I first looked into it. For most ancient writing, historians are thrilled to have a handful of copies made many centuries after the original. The works of the Roman historian Tacitus survive in very few manuscripts, the earliest copied something like eight hundred years after he wrote, and no serious person stays up at night doubting that Tacitus is roughly what Tacitus wrote. The New Testament, by contrast, survives in thousands of Greek manuscripts, plus thousands more in other ancient languages like Latin and Syriac, with some small fragments dating to within about a hundred years of the writing or even less. If you throw out the New Testament as hopelessly unreliable on manuscript grounds, you have to throw out essentially every other ancient text along with it, because nothing else from that era is even in the same neighborhood for documentation. That is not a Christian talking point. That is just how the documents physically stack up when you line them on a shelf.

So what about the changes that real, careful scholars admit do exist. This is where honesty matters, because there genuinely are differences among the manuscripts. Tens of thousands of them, in fact, and that scary number gets thrown around precisely because it sounds enormous. But you have to ask what kind of differences they are. The overwhelming majority are things like a misspelled word, a slip of word order in Greek that does not even change the meaning once you translate it into English, a doubled letter, or an obvious copying hiccup that the comparison method catches instantly. The number of differences that actually affect anything important is tiny, and the ones that do touch something are not hidden from you. Open up almost any decent modern Bible and you will find little footnotes that say things like, some early manuscripts do not include this verse. Stop and think about what that means. The translators are showing you their own work. They are pointing at the seams. They are not papering over the uncertain spots. A con artist hides the evidence and hopes you do not look. These people print the uncertain parts right there in the margin for a fifteen year old to read on a Tuesday. That is the opposite of a cover up. That is a confidence that the text can take the scrutiny.

Now the canon, the committee objection, the picture of men in robes voting on the truth and burning the rejects. The image most people carry, of a single council in a smoky room deciding what God said and torching everything else, is mostly a movie, not history. By the time any council formally listed the books, the core writings, the four Gospels and the letters of Paul, had already been read, copied, quoted, and treated as authoritative by churches scattered across the entire Mediterranean for generations. The councils were not inventing a list out of thin air and imposing it on a surprised church. They were recognizing, and finally writing down, what the wide and far flung community of believers had already been using and trusting for a long time. The rough test was something like this. Did this book trace back to the apostles or their close circle. Was it consistent with the faith that people were already living and dying for. And was it received broadly, across many churches, rather than embraced by one strange splinter group in one city. The books that did not make the cut, the later gospels people love to bring up in arguments, were mostly written much later, by groups with very different ideas about who Jesus was, and they read nothing at all like the earlier material when you actually open them. They were not banned bestsellers ripped from your hands. They were latecomers that the broad church never recognized as theirs in the first place.

Here is the part the telephone insult conveniently forgets to mention. The early Christians had every reason in the world to clean up their own scriptures, and they pointedly did not. If you were inventing a religion and you controlled the editing, you would never leave in the parts where the founder's closest friends look like fools. You would not keep the scene where Peter, the leader, denies even knowing Jesus three separate times in one night to save himself. You would not record that the very first witnesses to the resurrection were women, whose testimony was not even accepted as valid in the courts of that era, which is the last detail on earth you would fabricate if your goal was to convince that particular culture. You would not keep Jesus crying out from the cross that God had forsaken him. Made up propaganda gets sanded down smooth and flattering. These texts are full of splinters and embarrassments and loose ends. That roughness is a fingerprint. It is the fingerprint of people trying hard to preserve what actually happened rather than what would sell well.

So where does all of this leave you, honestly. Not at certainty about every single word, and I will not pretend otherwise. The honest position is this. The Bible is far better preserved and far better attested than almost anything else surviving from the ancient world. What it says now is overwhelmingly what it said at the very start. The few genuinely uncertain spots are openly marked for you rather than hidden away. And the books inside it were recognized over time by a wide and frequently divided community rather than dictated by one council with an agenda. That is a strong place to stand. It is not a magic place where doubt becomes illegal and questions get you in trouble. You can trust this book roughly the way you trust the best documented events of ancient history, which is to say a great deal, and still keep asking hard questions about the parts that trouble you.

And there are parts that will trouble you. There are passages that trouble me and have for years. But notice the difference between two separate questions. One question is whether the text reliably reaches you across the centuries, whether you are actually reading what was written. That question has a strong answer, and it is yes. A completely different question is whether you understand and agree with everything the text says once it gets to you. That second one is a lifetime of wrestling, and you are allowed to do both at once, to trust that you have the real words while you struggle with what some of them mean. Do not let anyone rush you past either part.

Where to take this. If the manuscript stuff grabbed you, read someone who lays it out carefully for normal people rather than scholars. Rebecca McLaughlin and Tim Keller both write about this without burying you under footnotes. If you want to feel the weight of the texts themselves rather than arguments about them, read one whole Gospel straight through in one or two sittings, Mark is the short fast one, and notice for yourself how unpolished and specific and strange it is, how unlike a smooth marketing document. And find someone who actually knows the history, a teacher or pastor or older friend who will not panic or get defensive when you bring up the telephone objection, and bring it to them directly. The answer holds up. It is completely okay to make it prove that it does.

chapters.title: Can You Trust the Bible?
chapters.summary: The Bible is not what most people think it is, defenders and critics alike. It is stranger, more varied, more honest, and more resilient than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines.
chapters.body:
The question "Can you trust the Bible?" is asked by two very different groups of people, and they mean two very different things by it. The skeptic means: Is this ancient collection of texts reliable in any meaningful sense, or is it a repository of myths, contradictions, and outdated moral frameworks that no educated person should take seriously? The anxious believer means: Can I still hold on to this book that shaped my faith, given everything I have learned about its composition, its history, its internal tensions, and the uses to which it has been put?

Both questions deserve honest answers. But honest answers require that we first establish what the Bible actually is, not the Bible of popular imagination, whether that imagination is fundamentalist or secularist, but the Bible as it actually exists: a sprawling, multi-voiced, internally diverse collection of texts written across more than a millennium by dozens of authors in multiple languages and genres, compiled and canonized through a centuries-long process of communal discernment, and read in wildly different ways by wildly different communities for two thousand years.

The first step toward trusting the Bible is to stop expecting it to be something it never claimed to be.

## A Library, Not a Book

The word "Bible" comes from the Greek *ta biblia*, "the books." The plural is not incidental. The Bible is a library: sixty-six books (in the Protestant canon; seventy-three in the Catholic; more in the Orthodox), written by more than forty authors over a span of roughly 1,500 years, in at least three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic, and Greek), across multiple continents and cultural contexts. It includes history, law, poetry, prophecy, wisdom literature, gospel narrative, epistolary correspondence, and apocalyptic vision. To read Genesis and Revelation as if they belong to the same genre is like reading a legal brief and a love poem as if they operate by the same rules.

The diversity of the biblical library is not a weakness to be apologized for. It is a feature to be understood. The Bible contains four Gospels, not one, and they do not always agree on the details of the events they narrate. Matthew and Luke give different genealogies for Jesus. Mark ends without resurrection appearances (in the earliest manuscripts). John includes events and discourses that the Synoptic Gospels do not mention. The early church knew this. It did not harmonize the Gospels into a single narrative. It kept all four, side by side, in a deliberate act of theological polyphony. The message was clear: the truth about Jesus requires more than one perspective to tell.

The Old Testament is similarly diverse. The Deuteronomistic history (Joshua through Kings) interprets Israel's story through the lens of covenant faithfulness: when Israel obeys God, it prospers; when it disobeys, it suffers. The book of Job dismantles that very framework, presenting a righteous man who suffers catastrophically and whose friends' insistence on the prosperity theology is explicitly condemned by God. Ecclesiastes pushes further, questioning whether the patterns of divine justice are discernible at all: "The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong." The Bible argues with itself. This is a sign of intellectual honesty, not incoherence.

## What Inerrancy Means and Does Not Mean

The doctrine of biblical inerrancy, as articulated in the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978), holds that the Bible, in its original manuscripts, is without error in all that it affirms. This is a more careful claim than it is often taken to be. The Chicago Statement itself includes important qualifications: it acknowledges that the Bible uses phenomenological language (the sun "rises"), approximations, and literary conventions; it affirms that genre must be taken into account; it denies that inerrancy requires strict literalism.

The problem is that the popular understanding of inerrancy has little to do with the Chicago Statement. In common usage, "inerrancy" has come to mean something like "every sentence of the Bible is a factual assertion that can be verified by modern standards of accuracy." This is not what the doctrine means, and treating it as such creates problems that the doctrine's careful formulators never intended. When a believer is told that inerrancy means the Bible cannot contain any factual discrepancy, and then discovers that the accounts of Paul's conversion in Acts 9, 22, and 26 differ in their details, the result is not a deeper faith but a crisis of faith, a crisis produced not by the Bible itself but by the expectations placed upon it.

A more robust understanding of biblical authority does not require inerrancy in the popular sense. It requires the conviction that the Bible is the primary and normative witness to God's self-revelation, that it is trustworthy in its central claims about God, humanity, sin, and salvation, and that it functions as the authoritative text of the Christian community for faith and practice. This is the view held by the vast majority of Christian tradition, Catholic, Orthodox, and much of Protestantism, and it does not depend on the absence of every historical or scientific difficulty.

## The Transmission Question

A common skeptical argument runs as follows: we do not have the original manuscripts of any biblical text; we have only copies of copies, separated from the originals by decades or centuries; therefore we cannot know what the originals said. This argument has a grain of truth and a mountain of distortion.

The grain of truth: we do not possess the autographs (original manuscripts) of any biblical text. The earliest complete manuscripts of the New Testament date to the fourth century, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus. The mountain of distortion: the textual evidence for the New Testament is vastly more abundant than for any other ancient text. We have approximately 5,800 Greek manuscripts, 10,000 Latin manuscripts, and thousands of manuscripts in other ancient languages. The earliest fragmentary manuscripts, such as P52, a fragment of John's Gospel, date to within a few decades of the original composition. By comparison, the earliest manuscript of Homer's *Iliad* dates to roughly 500 years after its composition, and we have fewer than 2,000 manuscripts of it. No classical scholar doubts that we can reconstruct Homer with reasonable accuracy. The textual evidence for the New Testament is orders of magnitude greater.

The field of textual criticism, the scholarly discipline devoted to reconstructing the original text from the available manuscripts, has produced a New Testament text that scholars across the theological spectrum regard as highly reliable. Bruce Metzger, perhaps the greatest textual critic of the twentieth century, estimated that the New Testament text is 99.5 percent certain, and that the remaining variants affect no significant doctrine. Bart Ehrman, Metzger's student and a prominent agnostic scholar, has acknowledged the reliability of the textual tradition even while disagreeing with its theological claims.

The variants that do exist are overwhelmingly minor, spelling differences, word-order changes, the kind of scribal errors one would expect in a hand-copied tradition. The handful of significant variants, the longer ending of Mark, the Johannine Comma (1 John 5:7-8), the story of the woman caught in adultery (John 7:53-8:11), are well known, are flagged in every modern translation, and do not affect any central Christian doctrine. The text of the Bible has been transmitted with a fidelity that is remarkable by the standards of the ancient world.

## Genre Matters

The single most important skill for reading the Bible honestly is the ability to recognize genre. Poetry is not history. Apocalypse is not prediction. Parable is not journalism. Law code is not systematic theology. When Jesus says, "If your right eye causes you to sin, tear it out," he is not prescribing self-mutilation. He is using hyperbole, a recognized rhetorical device, to make a point about the seriousness of moral compromise. When the psalmist writes, "The Lord is my shepherd," he is not making a zoological claim about God's profession. He is using metaphor to express trust in God's provision and care.

The creation accounts in Genesis 1-2 are a case study in the importance of genre. Genesis 1 is a highly structured, liturgical text, six days of creation arranged in two parallel triads (forming and filling), culminating in the Sabbath rest. It reads less like a scientific report and more like a hymn. Genesis 2 tells a different creation story with a different order of events (in Genesis 1, animals are created before humans; in Genesis 2, the man is created before the animals). Reading both as journalistic accounts of the same event creates an immediate contradiction. Reading them as two complementary theological narratives, one emphasizing the cosmic scope of God's creative work, the other emphasizing the intimacy of God's relationship with humanity, dissolves the contradiction and reveals the depth of both texts.

The prophetic literature is not primarily about predicting the future. It is about calling the present to account. When Isaiah says, "Your new moons and your appointed feasts my soul hates" (Isaiah 1:14), he is not making a prediction. He is delivering a divine indictment of a religious establishment that practices ritual without justice. Reading the prophets as a crystal ball for contemporary geopolitics, as much popular prophecy teaching does, is a fundamental misreading of the genre.

The book of Revelation, or the Apocalypse, is the most misread book in the Bible precisely because its genre is so unfamiliar to modern readers. Apocalyptic literature was a well-established genre in the ancient world, with recognizable conventions: symbolic numbers, cosmic imagery, beasts representing empires, a final confrontation between good and evil. First-century readers would have recognized these conventions instantly. Modern readers, unfamiliar with the genre, tend to read Revelation as a literal prediction of future events, an approach that produces endless speculation and very little understanding.

## The Bible the Bible Actually Is

The Bible we actually have is stranger, more honest, and more durable than either the fundamentalist or the skeptic imagines. It contains genealogies that do not match, numbers that do not add up, and laws that later biblical texts modify or set aside. It includes the Song of Solomon, which is an erotic love poem, and Ecclesiastes, which flirts with nihilism. It preserves the story of David, the man after God's own heart, committing adultery, arranging a murder, and being confronted by a prophet who tells him a parable to trick him into pronouncing his own judgment. It does not protect its heroes. It does not sanitize its history. It does not resolve its tensions into a neat systematic theology.

And it has endured. It has survived the Roman Empire's attempt to destroy it, the medieval church's attempt to control it, the Enlightenment's attempt to dismiss it, and the modern church's attempt to domesticate it. It has been translated into more than 700 languages. It has shaped the moral imagination of Western civilization, its concepts of human dignity, justice, care for the vulnerable, and the equality of persons before God have become so deeply embedded in Western thought that even secular people who reject the Bible's authority often hold values that are unintelligible apart from it.

## How to Read It Honestly

Reading the Bible honestly means reading it on its own terms. It means paying attention to genre, to historical context, to the literary conventions of the ancient world. It means acknowledging the tensions without flattening them and sitting with the difficulties without pretending they do not exist. It means recognizing that the Bible was written in specific historical contexts by authors who shared the cosmological assumptions of their time, a flat earth, a solid dome over the sky, a three-tiered universe, and that these assumptions are part of the cultural medium through which the theological message was communicated, not part of the message itself.

It also means refusing to read the Bible cynically. The skeptic who approaches the Bible looking only for contradictions and moral failures will find them. But this is a way of reading that refuses to hear what the text is actually saying, refuses to sit with the Sermon on the Mount, with the parable of the prodigal son, with the vision of the new heavens and the new earth, with the relentless biblical insistence that the God of the universe cares about the widow, the orphan, and the stranger. A hermeneutic of suspicion, applied without a corresponding hermeneutic of trust, is not honest reading. It is reading with a predetermined conclusion.

Can you trust the Bible? Not if you mean: can you treat it as a science textbook, a history textbook, or a systematic theology that dropped complete from heaven? No. But if you mean: can you trust it as the primary witness to God's self-revelation, as a text that has been tested by centuries of critical scrutiny and has survived, as the book that still has the power to name what is wrong with the world and point toward what would make it right, then yes. You can trust it. Not because it is simple, but because it is honest. And honest things are worth trusting, even when, especially when, they do not give us everything we wish they would.

chapters.title: Did the Resurrection Actually Happen?
chapters.summary: Everything Christians claim hangs on one event in one weekend, and you are allowed to ask whether it actually happened.
chapters.body:
Nobody tells you this when you are young and sitting in a pew. The whole thing rests on one weekend. Not on Jesus being a good teacher. Not on the Sermon on the Mount being beautiful, which it is. The entire structure of Christianity is loaded onto a single claim about a single Sunday morning. A man who was publicly executed, confirmed dead, and sealed in a tomb was alive again two days later. If that did not happen, then Paul himself says the whole thing is a waste of your one short life. He says it plainly. If Christ is not raised, your faith is useless. That is not a guy hedging his bets. That is a man betting everything on a fact.

So you are allowed to ask the question that probably makes the adults around you nervous. Did it actually happen, or is it a comforting story people tell at funerals because the alternative is unbearable. That is not a rebellious question. That is the most reasonable question in the building. The faith itself invites it.

Let me give you the objection in its strongest form, because if I hand you a weak version I am cheating you, and you will spot it. Dead people stay dead. You know this. You have been to a funeral, or you will be. The most universal, most tested, most exceptionless pattern any human being has ever observed is that when someone dies, they do not come back. Every single day, across all of recorded history, the data points the same direction. So when an ancient document claims a resurrection, the smart move is not to investigate, it is to assume the most ordinary explanation, because the most ordinary explanation is almost always the right one. People lie. People hallucinate when they are grieving. Legends grow over decades. Stories get better with each retelling. We know all of these things happen constantly because we watch them happen. We have never once verified a resurrection. So which is more likely. That the laws of biology broke for one Jewish carpenter, or that some heartbroken fishermen and a story got out of hand. Put that way, it sounds like the question answers itself before you even start.

That is the real objection, stated as strongly as I know how. Now let me show you why a lot of serious people, including some who set out to disprove the whole thing, found that the ordinary explanations do not actually hold together when you press on them with any weight.

Start with what almost everyone agrees on, because this surprises people. Even scholars who think the resurrection is a myth tend to grant a handful of facts, because the historical evidence for them is strong and granting them does not require believing in miracles. One, Jesus was really crucified by the Romans, who were extremely good at killing people and had no reason to do it halfway. Two, his tomb was found empty by his followers shortly afterward. Three, large numbers of people, individually and in groups, sincerely believed they had seen him alive again. Four, this belief turned a scattered, terrified group of failures into people who would rather die than take it back. These are not church slogans. These are the starting points most historians work from, religious or not. The argument among serious people is not really about these facts. The argument is about the best explanation for the facts. And that is exactly the right way to think about history. You do not prove an event the way you prove a triangle. You weigh the explanations and ask which one accounts for everything at once.

So go down the list of ordinary explanations and actually test them, the way you would test an alibi in a courtroom.

Maybe he did not really die. Maybe he just passed out on the cross and woke up later in the cool of the tomb. This one feels clever for about ten seconds, until you remember who did the killing. Roman soldiers executed people for a living. If a prisoner survived, the soldier paid for the mistake with his own life, so they were thorough. They drove a spear into his side specifically to confirm death. And even if you imagine a man surviving a Roman scourging, the crucifixion itself, and a spear wound to the torso, you then have to imagine that same shredded man rolling away a heavy stone from the inside, slipping past a guard, and then walking up to his friends and convincing them not that he needed a doctor, which he obviously would, but that he was the glorious conqueror of death. Nobody starts a world religion limping and bleeding. This theory asks you to swallow something harder to believe than the resurrection it was trying to replace.

Maybe they stole the body. This is the oldest counter theory of them all, and here is the fascinating part. It is recorded right inside the Gospels themselves. Which tells you something. It tells you the empty tomb was not in dispute even by the opponents. Both sides agreed the body was gone. The only argument was about why it was gone. But look hard at what the theft theory actually requires. It requires the disciples to knowingly steal a corpse, knowingly build a lie on top of it, and then knowingly suffer beatings, prison, torture, and execution for that lie, all of them, for the rest of their lives, with not one of them ever cracking under pressure and selling out the others to save his own skin. Think about people you know. People will absolutely die for something they sincerely believe is true. People do not generally die, one by one, in agony, for something they personally know they invented last Tuesday. Liars fold when the cost gets high enough. These men did not fold. The cost got as high as a cost can get, and they did not fold.

Maybe they hallucinated. Grief does strange things to the mind, and people who lose someone they love sometimes feel that person near, even sense them in a room. That is real, and it is gentle to consider. But hallucinations are private events. They happen inside one skull. They do not happen to five hundred people at once, as Paul claims happened, and they do not happen on cue to a hardened skeptic like James, the brother of Jesus, who did not even believe during Jesus' lifetime, or to Paul himself, who was actively on the road to arrest and imprison Christians when it happened to him. A detailed group experience, shared by hundreds, of eating with someone and touching him, is not a recognized psychological event. And there is a harder problem the hallucination theory cannot touch. A hallucination does not empty a tomb. Even if every last follower imagined the whole thing, the body would still have been lying right there in Jerusalem. And the authorities, who badly, desperately wanted this movement crushed, could have ended it in a single afternoon by marching the corpse through the streets. They never did. The simplest reason they never did is that they could not.

Maybe the legend just grew over time, the way fish stories grow with each telling. This is the strongest of the ordinary theories, so give it real respect. Stories do inflate across generations, and we have all watched it happen. But the resurrection claim is not late. The creed Paul quotes in First Corinthians fifteen, the formal list of witnesses, is something scholars across the spectrum, including skeptical ones, date to within just a few years of the crucifixion, possibly within months. That is nowhere near enough time for a legend to bury the facts, especially when the named eyewitnesses are still alive and walking around and could be questioned by anyone who wanted to check. Legends need the witnesses to die off first. These did not have that luxury. N. T. Wright, who has written more carefully on this than almost anyone alive, makes a point that is easy to miss. Nobody in that world was even expecting an individual resurrection in the middle of history. It was not a category their culture had. They believed, if anything, in a general resurrection of everyone at the end of time, not one person rising in the middle of an ordinary week. So they were not primed to invent this. They had no template for it. They had to be confronted with something that forced them to build brand new language to describe it.

Now stack it all up and look at the whole thing at once, because that is where the weight is. The tomb was empty, and the furious enemies of the movement never once produced a body to end it. The witnesses were many and varied, including a skeptic brother and a former persecutor, not just the inner circle who loved him. The followers transformed almost overnight from cowards hiding behind locked doors, terrified of being next, into people who walked into the very same city that had just executed their leader and announced out loud that he was alive, and then refused to stop saying it under threat of death, for decades. Something happened that weekend that turned total defeat into the most stubborn confidence in human history. The question is not whether something happened. Something clearly happened. The question is what is big enough to explain all of it together.

I am not going to hand you a bow on top of this. Here is the honest part. None of this is a mathematical proof, and anyone who tells you it is, is selling you something, so be careful with them. History does not work like geometry. It works like a courtroom. You weigh the evidence, you look at the alternatives, and you ask what explanation makes the most sense of everything at once. You will always be able to construct some story where it did not happen, the same way a determined person can construct a story where any historical event did not happen. The real question is not whether such a story is possible. It is whether you are believing the more reasonable thing or the less reasonable thing.

What I can tell you is that the lazy version of skepticism, the one that says of course it did not happen, do not even bother looking, is not actually the brave or the smart position. It just feels like it because it is the one in the air around you. The genuinely brave position is to look. To read the alternatives carefully and notice that each one quietly breaks under its own weight when you lean on it. To sit with the strange, stubborn fact that a movement built on a dead leader should have died with him in a week, and instead it outlived the empire that killed him, the empire that eventually bent the knee to the carpenter it had crucified.

Where to take this. Do not let me, or a youth pastor, or a confident voice on the internet be the last word on something this large. Read someone who argues it carefully and respects your intelligence. Rebecca McLaughlin writes for people exactly your age who are asking exactly this question. N. T. Wright goes much deeper if you want the long version and have the patience for it. And find one adult who will not flinch when you push hard on it, and push on it out loud, to their face. A faith that cannot survive your hardest question was never worth having in the first place. This one has survived sharper questions than yours for two thousand years. It can survive being looked at by you.

chapters.title: Doesn't Science Disprove God?
chapters.summary: You have been told science and faith are at war, but the history and the actual questions are stranger than the slogan.
chapters.body:
You absorbed this one without anyone ever sitting you down to teach it. It is just in the air you breathe. Science is the grownup table, the serious place where you prove things, check them, run them again, and admit it when you turn out to be wrong. Faith is the kids table, the place where you believe stuff because it makes you feel safe and nobody is allowed to ask you for evidence. And the story goes that as science has marched steadily forward, explaining lightning and disease and the origin of the species one by one, it has slowly shoved God out of every hiding place he used to occupy, until now there is basically nothing left for him to do. So the smart, modern, honest thing is to let science have the truth and let religion keep the feelings and the holidays.

Let me give that its strongest form, because I do not want to be soft on it. Science makes testable predictions and then actually checks them against reality, mercilessly, and it has been right about an astonishing number of things. It put human beings on the moon and built the glowing rectangle in your pocket that you would not trade for anything. Religion, the objection says, makes claims that cannot be tested even in principle, and it has a long, embarrassing habit of retreating every single time science finally explains something that used to be a sacred mystery. It used to be that God personally moved the planets across the sky, and then Newton came along and showed it was gravity and math. It used to be that God hand crafted each animal in its present form, and then Darwin showed a mechanism that did not seem to need him. So why on earth would you place your bet on the side that keeps losing ground, decade after decade. Eventually, the argument concludes, God is just a name we give to the shrinking pile of things we have not gotten around to explaining yet.

That argument feels strong, and parts of it deserve real respect. Now let me show you the places where it quietly cheats.

Start with the war itself, because the bedrock assumption that science and faith have always been sworn enemies is, ironically, terrible history. The dramatic picture of brave, clear eyed scientists battling against ignorant church goons who hate knowledge and burn books is mostly a story that got invented in the eighteen hundreds by a small number of writers with a specific axe to grind, and historians of science have been quietly dismantling that picture for decades now. Here is the part that should genuinely surprise you and that nobody mentions. Modern science was largely born inside a Christian culture, built in significant part by people who believed in God, and a striking number of them said openly that their faith was the very reason they expected the universe to be understandable in the first place. Sit with that for a second. To do science at all, before you run a single experiment, you have to assume that the universe runs on consistent, rational laws that a human mind is actually capable of grasping. But why would you assume that. If the universe is just random churning matter with nothing behind it, why on earth would you expect it to be orderly, lawful, and elegant enough to write clean equations about. The early scientists had a reason for the assumption built right into their worldview. They believed a rational God had made an orderly world and had given human beings minds capable of reading it. Newton, Kepler, Faraday, Pascal himself, the people who built the whole enterprise from the ground up, were not sneaking science past their faith like contraband. They genuinely thought they were studying the handiwork of a mind. You are free to disagree with their conclusions. But you cannot honestly say that science grew up as the enemy of belief. It grew up, in large part, inside belief's own house, eating at its table.

Now the deeper move, and this is the single most important thing I want you to take from this whole article, because it will serve you for the rest of your life and in a hundred conversations. Science and faith are not two rival answers competing to solve the same question. They are answers to fundamentally different kinds of questions, and confusing the two is the exact place where the entire muddle comes from.

Science is spectacularly, world changingly good at answering how questions. How does a cell divide. How did these particular chemicals combine. How does gravity bend space and time. It tells you the mechanism, the process, the unbroken chain of physical causes. What science is simply not built to answer, by its own honest design and the design of every scientist worth the name, is the why and the should and the what for. Take the most loaded example imaginable. Suppose, for the sake of argument, that science one day gives you a complete, flawless, gap free account of how the universe began and how life developed, every single step laid out with no missing pieces. Notice carefully that you still have not touched the questions that actually keep human beings awake at three in the morning. Why is there something rather than nothing at all. Is my life worth anything or not. Is there such a thing as genuine right and wrong, or just things various creatures happen to prefer. Should I be kind even when being kind costs me badly. No experiment in any lab can reach a single one of those. Not because science is weak or failing, but because those are not how questions, and how is the only kind of question its tools can even pick up. A thermometer cannot weigh you. That is not a defect in the thermometer that better engineering will someday fix. It is just not the thing a thermometer is for.

Think about a paperback novel sitting on your desk. You could, in principle, give a complete and perfectly true physical account of that book. The exact chemistry of the ink, the wood pulp fibers in the paper, the precise wavelengths of light bouncing off each page into your eye. Every word of that account could be flawlessly accurate. And you would have said exactly nothing about what the story means, whether it is any good, or why it made you cry at the end. The physical description does not compete with the meaning of the story. It runs underneath it, quietly, while the meaning happens at a completely different level. Believers say that God is something like the author standing behind the entire story, not a character squeezed in somewhere inside it competing for elbow room with the other characters. So when science explains a mechanism, it is not crossing God off a list one item at a time. It is reading another sentence of his book aloud. Finding out exactly how the printing press worked does not make the author of the novel vanish into thin air.

That, by the way, is also precisely why the God of the gaps move, the strategy of betting on God to explain whatever science has not figured out yet, is a genuinely bad bet, and honestly believers should stop making it because it keeps blowing up in their faces. If your only reason to believe is the current list of unsolved scientific mysteries, then yes, of course, your faith is going to shrink a little every single time a clever scientist solves one of them. But that was never supposed to be the strong reason. The strong reason was never the gaps in the picture. It was the existence of the picture at all. The brute fact that there is anything whatsoever rather than nothing. That it turned out to be orderly instead of chaotic. That it is beautiful in ways it did not need to be. That you, a clump of atoms, can understand it and ask about it. Those do not shrink when a gap gets filled.

Which brings me to the one place where the science itself has gotten genuinely strange in a direction worth your attention. It is called fine tuning. Over the last century or so, physicists kept noticing that the basic numbers built into the fabric of the universe, the strength of gravity, the force that holds the nucleus of an atom together, the rate at which the universe expanded in the first instants after it began, all sit within unbelievably narrow ranges. Nudge several of those numbers by a hair in either direction and you do not get a slightly different universe with different scenery. You get no stars, no chemistry, no atoms heavier than hydrogen, no possibility of life anywhere, ever, at all. The settings appear tuned to a precision that is genuinely hard to put into ordinary words. This is not a religious claim being smuggled in. Physicists who believe absolutely nothing about God say it openly, and many of them find it deeply puzzling and want an explanation. There are basically three ways to take it. You can shrug and say it is just a staggering, cosmic accident and leave it there. You can guess that there are countless other universes we cannot see or test, so it is no real surprise that one of them happened to get lucky, though notice that is a very large thing to believe with no evidence you could ever check. Or you can say that it looks tuned because it actually was tuned, by something with intention. Now, fine tuning does not prove God, and I am not going to overplay it the way some eager people do. But notice exactly what it does accomplish. It means that the idea of a mind standing behind the universe is not some embarrassing leftover that science has cornered and is about to finish off. It is a live, serious option that thoughtful scientists, believers and skeptics alike, take seriously and argue about. The arrow is not all pointing in one direction.

So here is the honest landing, with no overclaiming on my part. Science does not disprove God, and it was never built to even try, because the existence of God is not a how question, and how is the only thing science can measure. The famous war between them is mostly a myth invented for other reasons, and the people who actually built science largely did not believe in that war and would have been baffled by it. What science does, magnificently, is describe the intricate machinery of a universe that, the more closely we examine it, looks more surprising and more finely set than anyone ever expected it to. You can look at the whole thing and conclude there is nothing at all behind the curtain. Plenty of brilliant, honest people do exactly that, and you should respect them. But that is not the only intelligent conclusion available, and any person who tells you that science has simply settled the God question and closed the file does not actually understand what science is for or what it can do.

Where to take this. If your real worry underneath all of this is evolution and the opening chapters of Genesis, know that serious, thoughtful Christians hold a genuine range of views on how those two things fit together, and you do not have to pick a final side on it this week or this year. If the fine tuning stuff grabbed you, read someone careful who will not oversell it. Rebecca McLaughlin walks through it for normal people, and there are real working scientists who are also Christians, like Francis Collins, who led the enormous project that mapped the entire human genome, who write directly about exactly this tension from the inside. And do this one concrete thing. The next time someone confidently tells you that science has disproved God, ask them a single, calm question. Which experiment, exactly, was it that tested and disproved it. Then watch what happens to the conversation. The question is far more honest than the slogan it interrupts.

chapters.title: Hasn't the Church Done Terrible Things?
chapters.summary: The crimes committed under the banner of Christ are real and many, and any honest defense of the faith has to own them before it says anything else.
chapters.body:
I am not going to begin this by minimizing anything, because the minimizing is part of the offense. The church has blessed slave ships. It has burned dissenters. It has run residential schools that stripped children of their language and their families, sometimes their lives. It has covered for men who abused children and moved them to fresh parishes to abuse again. It has baptized empire, justified conquest, and called the spoils a mission. These are not slanders invented by the faith's enemies. They are facts, many of them documented by the church's own records, and a Christianity that cannot say so plainly is not worth defending.

The objection built on this is simple and devastating. If Christianity were true, if it actually changed people and connected them to a holy God, you would expect its followers to be conspicuously better than everyone else. Instead they have often been worse, or at least no better, and sometimes the institution itself has been the engine of the cruelty. So either the faith does not do what it claims, or the claim is false. Look at the fruit, the objection says, and judge the tree.

That is a serious argument and it has a true premise inside it. Jesus Himself said you will know them by their fruit. He invited exactly this scrutiny. So the question is not whether the church's crimes count against it. They do, and a believer who waves them away has not understood his own scriptures. The question is what, precisely, they count against, and whether they count against the thing the faith actually claims or against a thing it does not claim.

Start with the most important and least comfortable point. Christianity is the one major worldview whose own founding documents predict and explain exactly this failure. The faith does not teach that its followers are good people who have arrived. It teaches the opposite, that they are people who have admitted they are not good, who needed rescue precisely because they could not make themselves righteous. The church is, by its own description, a hospital for the morally sick, not a museum of the morally finished. So when you find sin inside it, you have not found a contradiction of the message. You have found the message confirmed in the ugliest possible way. The men who ran the inquisitions were not too Christian. By the standard their own book gives them, they were not Christian enough, and the book says so to their faces. Whatever Jesus taught, He did not teach men to burn heretics, and the verses they would have had to ignore to do it are not obscure.

Now, the skeptic can rightly object that this is too convenient. If good behavior proves the faith and bad behavior also proves the faith, since the faith predicted bad behavior, then nothing could ever count against it, and a theory that cannot be falsified is not telling you anything. This is a fair philosophical complaint and I do not want to slide past it. So let me name what would actually count against Christianity. It would count against the faith if Christianity produced no real saints, if it never moved anyone toward sacrificial love, if its teaching, faithfully followed, made people crueler. That is the test, and it is a test the faith can fail in principle. The honest comparison is not between Christians and angels. It is between what people did when they followed the teaching and what they did when they violated it. The Crusader killing in the name of Christ was disobeying Christ. The abolitionist freeing slaves in the name of Christ was obeying Him. Both quoted the same book. Only one was reading it rightly, and we can tell which, because the book is not actually ambiguous about whether you should massacre a city or whether you should love your enemy.

There is a sharper version of this worth stating, because skeptics sometimes reply that anyone can read anything they want out of a text, that the abolitionist and the slaveholder both found their case in the same book, so the book settles nothing. But this is not quite true, and the history shows it. The slaveholder had to work hard, had to lean on a handful of verses ripped from their setting and ignore the thundering arc of the whole story, a story that begins with a people freed from slavery and is organized around a God who hears the cry of the oppressed. The abolitionist did not have to strain. He had the grain of the thing running with him, the image of God in every person, the leveling truth that in Christ there is neither slave nor free. When two readers disagree and one has to suppress the central message to make his case while the other rides it, that is not a tie. It is a tell. The text is not infinitely pliable. It pushed, over centuries and against enormous economic interest, in one direction, and the people who finally won the argument won it with the book, not against it.

This points to something the objection usually leaves out, which is the other half of the ledger. The same tradition that produced inquisitors also produced the people who built the first hospitals, who founded universities, who took in the infants left to die on Roman hillsides, who led the charge against the slave trade, who ran the underground railroad, who marched in Birmingham with scripture on their lips. The man who did more than any other to end the British slave trade, William Wilberforce, did it as an act of explicit Christian conviction, against a slaving establishment that was itself nominally Christian. The civil rights movement in America was not a secular movement that happened to use churches. It was a church movement, led by pastors, grounded in the claim that every person bears the image of God. You cannot tell the story of human rights without telling the story of people who got the idea that humans have inviolable worth from somewhere, and a great deal of that somewhere is the conviction that every person is made in the image of a God who loves them.

There is a further point that the skeptic, to be consistent, has to face. The very standard by which we condemn the church's crimes is, in large part, a standard the church taught the world. When we say the Crusades were evil, that slavery was an abomination, that abusing the vulnerable is among the worst things a person can do, we are appealing to the dignity of the individual, the priority of the weak, the wrongness of using power to crush the powerless. Those are not the natural values of every culture and every age. The ancient world did not believe the weak had special claims. It believed the strong were entitled to rule the weak, and that exposing unwanted infants and crucifying slaves were simply how the world worked. The idea that the powerful owe something to the powerless, that the victim has moral priority over the conqueror, came into Western consciousness largely through a faith that worshiped a crucified victim. So when people use the language of the victim to condemn the church, they are often, without knowing it, using the church's own deepest teaching against the church's worst behavior. That is not a defense of the behavior. It is a clue about where the moral measuring stick came from.

There is a comparison the objection usually avoids, and fairness requires making it, though carefully. The twentieth century ran a kind of experiment in what happens when societies deliberately threw off the Christian framework and built on something else. The regimes that set out to abolish religion and remake humanity on a purely material basis, in Russia and China and Cambodia, produced killing on a scale that dwarfs every religious atrocity in history combined, tens of millions dead in a few decades. I raise this not to score a point, because atheists did not kill in the name of atheism the way crusaders killed in the name of Christ, and the comparison can be abused. The honest lesson is narrower and more sobering for everyone. The capacity for monstrous evil is not located in religion. It is located in the human heart, and it will use whatever banner is available, the cross or the hammer or the flag or the race. The believer who thinks his faith makes him safe from it has not read his own scriptures, which say the line between good and evil runs through every human being, starting with him. Christianity does not claim to have found the good people. It claims to have diagnosed, more accurately than any rival, why there are no good people, and what it would cost to change that.

But I do not want to let the faith off with a clever reversal, because the wound is real and recent. The abuse scandals are not medieval. They are the lifetime of people reading this. Institutions that should have protected children protected themselves instead, and did it while claiming the name of Christ, and the damage to faith those crimes caused is incalculable and largely deserved. There is no argument that heals that. The only honest response is the one the faith's own teaching demands, which is confession without excuse, repentance with restitution, and the recognition that judgment, as the New Testament says, begins with the household of God. A church that responds to its crimes with public relations rather than repentance has compounded the sin. The right Christian response to the church's evil is not defensiveness. It is grief, and the resolve to be different, and the willingness to say plainly that those who did these things in Christ's name betrayed Him.

So where does this leave the original objection. It leaves it true and incomplete. True, because the church really has done terrible things and a faith that denies it is lying. Incomplete, because the terrible things are violations of the faith's own teaching, not expressions of it, and because the same faith has produced an enormous amount of the world's mercy, and because the standard we use to judge the crimes was substantially shaped by the faith we are judging. The fruit is mixed because the field is mixed, because the church is full of unfinished people, and the faith said so from the start.

There is a question I would put back to the honest skeptic, not as a trap but because it is the question that turned me when I was outside all of this. Suppose you cleared away every false believer, every hypocrite, every institution that used Christ as a cover for power. Suppose you got down to the actual teaching and the actual man at the center of it. Would the problem be that He asks too little of you, or too much. The complaint against the church is almost always that it failed to live up to its founder. That is a strange complaint to make against a religion, and a revealing one. We do not usually fault a movement for falling short of a standard we think is worthless. We fault it for falling short of a standard we suspect, somewhere in us, is true. The hypocrisy of Christians is real. It is also, oddly, a backhanded testimony to the height of the thing they failed to reach.

chapters.title: How Can a Loving God Send Anyone to Hell?
chapters.summary: The doctrine of hell strikes most people as the cruelest thing Christianity teaches, and the objection deserves a real answer rather than a flinch.
chapters.body:
Of everything Christianity asks people to believe, hell is the teaching that makes them want to leave the room. It is not merely hard. It seems monstrous. A God of infinite love, we are told, will consign people to infinite torment for finite sins committed in a few short decades, often by people who never had a fair chance. Stated that way, it is not a doctrine you defend. It is a doctrine you flee. And I want to begin by saying that if that statement were an accurate account of what the faith teaches, fleeing would be the right response.

Let me give the objection its full force, because it has several parts and each one bites. First, the punishment seems wildly out of proportion. No human court would torture a thief forever, yet hell is endless. Second, it seems to make God into something worse than the cruelest tyrant, a being who creates conscious creatures knowing He will torment most of them without end. Third, it seems to corrupt the believer, because anyone who can be at peace in heaven while others scream below has had something human burned out of him. These are not cheap shots. The most serious people who have left the faith often point here, and they are not being shallow. They are being moral. The objection is, at its root, a moral protest, and that should make a Christian listen rather than argue, because the protest is reaching for something true.

Now let me try to say what the doctrine actually is, because much of the horror attaches to a cartoon. Start with the protest itself. When you recoil at the idea of injustice done to the undeserving, you are appealing to a standard of justice. You are saying some things are so wrong that they must be answered, that a universe where evil is simply shrugged off would be intolerable. Hold onto that, because it is the very intuition the doctrine of judgment is built on. A God who looked at genocide, at the trafficking of children, at a lifetime of cruelty, and felt nothing, did nothing, let it all evaporate into nothing at death, would not be loving. He would be morally asleep. The same heart that protests hell also protests a God who would not judge at all. We want evil answered. Judgment is the name for evil being answered. The question is not whether there should be justice. The question is what its shape and limits are.

Before going further, sit with how unusual it is that we even have this objection. The complaint that endless punishment is disproportionate assumes a scale of justice in which punishments should fit crimes, in which mercy is better than cruelty, in which the suffering of a person is a serious matter that the universe owes an accounting for. Where did that scale come from? Many cultures across history would have found the objection strange, would have shrugged at the suffering of the conquered or the low-born as simply the way of things. The conviction that every person's fate matters infinitely, that justice must be proportionate, that cruelty is an offense against the order of reality, is not the universal default. It is, to a remarkable degree, an inheritance from the very tradition being put on trial. The objector is borrowing the faith's own ledger to audit the faith's own books, which does not settle the question but should make us slow to assume the objection floats free of everything Christianity taught the world to value.

So consider the nature of the offense, the proportion problem. The usual picture is of God punishing trivial sins with infinite severity, and if sin were trivial the objection would stand. But the Christian claim is that sin is not first a matter of breaking rules. It is the rupture of a relationship with the source of all life and goodness, a turning away from the One in whom everything holds together. The gravity of a wrong is measured partly by the one wronged. Tear a stranger's photograph and it is rude. Tear your mother's only photograph of her dead son and you have done something far heavier, though the paper is the same. Sin against the infinite God is not infinite because we are important. It is grave because He is. That does not by itself prove the duration of hell, but it dissolves the cartoon of a cosmic overreaction to small things.

Now the deeper move, the one Lewis made and Tim Keller after him, and the one that changes the whole picture. The most serious Christian thinking does not describe hell as God dragging unwilling people into a torture chamber. It describes hell as God, in the end, honoring the choice a person has spent a lifetime making, the choice to be his own god, to live without the real one. Lewis said the doors of hell are locked on the inside. He meant that hell is what the freedom to refuse God finally becomes when it is allowed to have its way forever. A person can spend a life narrowing inward, building a self that wants no master, and God will not, at the last, override that. He takes our freedom seriously enough to let it succeed. Hell, on this view, is not God refusing to let people out. It is God refusing to force people in. The gates are locked from within.

This reframes the objection without dodging it. The doubter pictures a person pounding on hell's door begging to be let into heaven while God laughs. That picture is not the historic teaching and not, I think, the reality. The far stranger and more sober claim is that the person in hell does not want what heaven is. Heaven is the unfiltered presence of the God he organized his entire existence around avoiding. To that self, heaven would be the torment. Keller put it sharply. He said hell is just one's freely chosen identity apart from God on a trajectory into infinity. We see the early version of this in ordinary life, the person who has chosen resentment for so long that he can no longer enjoy anyone's happiness, who would rather be right and alone than reconciled. Run that out forever. That is the warning.

The skeptic can press back, and the strongest counter deserves room. He can say this is too neat, that real people are mixtures, that almost no one is a pure refuser, that plenty of people would gladly take God if He were on offer in terms they could accept. This is fair, and it is why Christians have always insisted that judgment belongs to God alone and not to us, precisely because only He can read a human heart to its floor. We are spectacularly bad at it. We write people off who are not finished and excuse people who are. The doctrine of judgment is not a license to sort our neighbors into the saved and the damned. It is a warning aimed first at the one reading it. Whenever the New Testament talks about judgment, it almost never lets you apply it to someone else. It turns it back on you. Examine yourself.

There is a third part of the objection that deserves its own answer, the charge that the doctrine corrupts the believer, that anyone capable of enjoying heaven while others suffer has had his humanity burned out. This is the sharpest version and it has worried serious Christians too. But notice the assumption inside it, that the person in heaven would look down on the lost as strangers whose fate is no concern of his. That is not the Christian hope. The hope is of a people remade, more loving than they are now and not less, more pained by loss and not numbed to it. If anything, the redeemed would feel the tragedy of a refused God more keenly than we do, not less, the way a healed person feels the wrongness of sickness more sharply than the sick. The Christian does not look forward to a heaven where he has stopped caring. He looks forward to a justice and a mercy so complete that, when finally seen whole, it does not require him to stop caring in order to be at peace. How those two things meet is beyond what I can draw for you. But the cartoon of the smug saved gloating over the damned is a thing the faith condemns, not a thing it teaches.

There is the matter of duration, the endlessness, which troubles many honest believers and not only skeptics. I will be candid that faithful Christians have held more than one view here, and Scripture is less explicit than the popular imagination assumes. Some read the language of destruction as meaning exactly that, that the finally unrepentant cease to be rather than suffer forever. Others hold the traditional view. The tradition has more room in it than the cartoon allows, and a person can take the warnings of judgment with full seriousness without committing to the most lurid version. What no faithful reading allows is the comfortable assumption that nothing is at stake, that all roads arrive at the same place and the choices of a life carry no final weight. The whole drama of the Bible insists that what you do with God matters, ultimately and forever. That is the hard floor under every softer reading.

And there is something the objection always leaves out, the thing that changes its entire register. The God who warns of judgment is the God who walked directly into it. The cross is the place where the One with every right to judge took the judgment Himself. Christianity does not teach a God who sits at a safe distance condemning the guilty. It teaches a God who came down into the dock, who absorbed in His own body the verdict we had earned, who did for us at infinite cost the one thing we could not do for ourselves.
