The claim is that what God has done in Jesus is the fullest and most decisive revelation of God's character and purposes, and that this revelation, because it happened in history, must be communicated through history: through witness, through community, through the messy, imperfect, often unfaithful process of human beings telling other human beings what they have seen and heard. The particularity of the gospel is not a limitation on God's love. It is a consequence of God's decision to work through history rather than around it.

## The Gospel as Public Truth

Lesslie Newbigin, the British missionary and theologian who spent decades in India before returning to a secularized England, argued that the gospel must be understood not as a private religious preference but as public truth, a claim about the way things actually are, a claim that has consequences for all of life, not just the "religious" part of life.

In his landmark work *The Gospel in a Pluralist Society* (1989), Newbigin observed that Western culture had developed a fatal dichotomy between "facts" (the domain of science, publicly verifiable, universally binding) and "values" (the domain of religion, privately held, not subject to public adjudication). In this framework, religious beliefs are relegated to the category of personal preference, like a taste in music or a choice of diet. You may believe in Jesus the way you believe in the superiority of jazz, but you cannot claim that your belief is true in the same way that the law of gravity is true.

Newbigin argued that this dichotomy is incoherent. The gospel makes claims about history, about the nature of reality, about the human condition, claims that are either true or false, not merely preferred or not preferred. To say "Jesus is Lord" is not to express a private religious sentiment. It is to make a claim about who actually rules the universe. And that claim either corresponds to reality or it does not. If it does, it has implications for politics, economics, education, science, art, and every other domain of human activity. It is not a private matter. It is the most public matter imaginable.

The challenge for Christians is to hold this conviction without arrogance, to claim that the gospel is true without claiming that they possess the truth in its entirety, to proclaim Christ without demonizing those who do not follow Christ, to hold firm convictions with genuine humility. This is not easy. The history of Christianity is littered with examples of conviction without humility, crusades, inquisitions, forced conversions, cultural imperialism. These failures are real, and they must be owned.

## Conviction Without Arrogance

The question of how to hold conviction without arrogance is not merely a tactical question about interfaith relations. It is a theological question at the heart of the gospel itself. If salvation is by grace, if the Christian's relationship with God is a gift, not an achievement, then the Christian has no grounds for superiority over anyone. The person who has been forgiven much has no basis for looking down on the person who has not yet received forgiveness. The proper posture of the Christian toward the non-Christian is not condescension but gratitude, the gratitude of one who has received what they did not deserve and cannot take credit for.

Karl Barth, in his theology of election, insisted that God's grace in Christ is directed not toward a select few but toward all of humanity. The church's role is not to be the exclusive club of the saved but the community that knows and proclaims what God has done for everyone. The church does not own God's grace. It witnesses to it. And a witness who behaves as though the good news belongs to them rather than to the one they are testifying about has misunderstood the nature of testimony.

## The Lived Test

There is a final criterion that operates below the level of formal argument, and it must be named. The ultimate test of a religious claim is not only whether it is intellectually coherent or historically grounded. It is whether it can bear the weight of an actual human life, with all its suffering, failure, ambiguity, and need. The question is not merely "Is this true?" but "Can I live this? Can this carry me through the worst night I will ever face? Can this make sense of the evil I have witnessed and the evil I have done?"

I have watched the gospel do that work. I have watched it sustain people through the death of children, the collapse of marriages, the destruction of careers, the slow dismantling of health. I have watched it reach into the lives of addicts, of prisoners, of the terminally ill, and offer something that no philosophical system and no therapeutic technique could provide, not a solution but a presence, not a program but a person, not an explanation for suffering but a companion in it who has himself suffered. I have watched people who had every reason to abandon their faith hold on to it, not because they were credulous but because the one they trusted had proven trustworthy in the darkest rooms of their lives.

This is not an argument that would satisfy a philosopher. It is a testimony that satisfies a pastor. And I offer it not as proof but as evidence, the kind of evidence that accumulates not in journals but in hospital rooms and living rooms and gravesides, in the places where abstractions collapse and only the real survives.

Why Christianity and not something else? Not because Christians are better people, they manifestly are not. Not because the church has a spotless record, it manifestly does not. Not because other traditions have nothing to teach, they manifestly do. But because Christianity makes claims that, if true, change everything: that the God who made the universe entered it in person, that this God died and rose again, that this God offers reconciliation as a gift rather than demanding it as an achievement, and that this gift is not a private religious experience but the truth about the way things actually are.

I hold these claims as a man who has been wrong about many things and may yet be wrong about more. I hold them not with the certainty of one who has figured everything out but with the trust of one who has been found by something, someone, too real and too costly to walk away from. That is not proof. It is testimony. And testimony is all any of us has.

chapters.title: Why Does God Allow Suffering?
chapters.summary: The problem of suffering is not an intellectual puzzle to be solved. It is a wound that demands not explanation but presence, and the Christian answer begins at the cross, where God enters the wound.
chapters.body:
The question arrives not in a seminar room but in a hospital corridor. It arrives at 2:00 a.m. when the phone rings with the news that reshapes everything. It arrives in the oncologist's office, in the aftermath of the hurricane, in the silence that follows the funeral of a child who should have outlived every adult in the room. "Why does God allow suffering?" is the most human question ever asked, and anyone who answers it too quickly has not understood the question.

I have been a pastor for fifteen years. I have sat in rooms where the question was not academic. I have held the hands of parents burying their children, of spouses burying their partners, of people whose suffering was so acute and so undeserved that any theological explanation would have been an obscenity. I will not pretend that I have an answer that makes suffering acceptable. What I have is a set of responses, philosophical, theological, biblical, pastoral, that I believe are honest, even where they are incomplete. Especially where they are incomplete.

## The Problem Stated Honestly

The problem of evil is the oldest and most powerful objection to belief in God. Epicurus framed it with a precision that has never been improved upon: if God is willing to prevent evil but unable, God is not omnipotent; if God is able but unwilling, God is not good; if God is both able and willing, evil should not exist; but evil exists. Therefore, either God is not omnipotent, or God is not good, or God does not exist.

David Hume, in his *Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion* (1779), put the argument in the mouth of Philo, the skeptic: "Is the world, considered in general, and as it appears to us in this life, different from what a man or such a limited being would, beforehand, expect from a very powerful, wise, and benevolent deity?" The answer, Hume suggested, was obvious. No one looking at the world with fresh eyes, at its earthquakes and cancers, its famines and genocides, its random cruelties inflicted on the innocent, would conclude that it was the product of a being that was both all-powerful and all-good.

J.L. Mackie, in his 1955 essay "Evil and Omnipotence," formalized the argument as a logical inconsistency. The following three propositions, Mackie argued, cannot all be true simultaneously: God is omnipotent, God is wholly good, and evil exists. At least one must be false. If God exists, God is either not omnipotent or not good. The only way to hold all three is to introduce some additional premise that resolves the contradiction, which is precisely what theodicy attempts to do.

The argument is not merely philosophical. It is existential. Fyodor Dostoevsky, in the "Rebellion" chapter of *The Brothers Karamazov* (1880), put it in the mouth of Ivan Karamazov, who catalogs cases of cruelty to children, a girl locked in an outhouse in the cold by her parents, a boy torn apart by a general's hunting dogs, and then delivers his verdict: even if all of this suffering is somehow necessary for the final harmony of the universe, even if it produces some ultimate good that justifies every tear, he refuses to accept it. "It's not God I don't accept," Ivan says. "It's the world he created." He returns his ticket to divine harmony. The suffering of children is too high a price.

Elie Wiesel, in *Night* (1960), described the hanging of a boy in Auschwitz and the whispered question from the crowd: "Where is God now?" The answer, Wiesel wrote, came from within him: "Here he is, hanging on this gallows." Whatever else one does with that sentence, one must not domesticate it into a tidy theological resolution. It is a scream.

## The Free Will Defense

The most influential philosophical response to the logical problem of evil was developed by Alvin Plantinga in *God, Freedom, and Evil* (1974). Plantinga argued that God's omnipotence does not include the ability to do the logically impossible. Creating beings with genuine free will and simultaneously guaranteeing that those beings will never choose evil is a logical contradiction, like creating a round square. If God values free creatures, creatures capable of love, moral choice, and genuine relationship, then God must permit the possibility that those creatures will use their freedom for evil.

Plantinga's argument is widely regarded, even by atheist philosophers, as having resolved the logical problem of evil. Mackie himself acknowledged that the free will defense showed the three propositions are not logically inconsistent. But the argument has significant limitations. It addresses moral evil, the suffering caused by human choices, but it does not address natural evil: the earthquake that kills thousands, the childhood leukemia, the tsunami that does not discriminate between the guilty and the innocent. No human free will chose the tectonic plates into motion.

Some theologians have extended the free will defense to natural evil by invoking the regularity of natural law. A world in which fire warms but never burns, in which gravity sustains life but never kills, in which bacteria nourish but never infect, would be a world without consistent natural laws, and therefore a world in which rational action, scientific inquiry, and moral development would be impossible. Richard Swinburne has argued along these lines: a world regular enough to permit meaningful human action must also be a world in which natural processes sometimes cause suffering. The argument has force, but it does not comfort the parents of the child swept away in the flood.

## The Soul-Making Theodicy

The soul-making theodicy, rooted in the theology of Irenaeus of Lyon (second century) and developed by the philosopher John Hick in *Evil and the God of Love* (1966), offers a different framework. The Augustinian tradition understood evil as a consequence of the Fall, a corruption of an originally perfect creation. The Irenaean tradition understands creation not as a finished product that was ruined but as an ongoing project in which human beings are created immature and are being shaped, through the challenges and sufferings of life, into the likeness of God.

On this view, the world is not a paradise that was lost. It is a soul-making environment, a place where courage, compassion, perseverance, forgiveness, and love can be forged precisely because they are costly. Courage without danger is not courage. Compassion without suffering is not compassion. Forgiveness without genuine offense is not forgiveness. The qualities that constitute human maturity and moral depth cannot be produced in a world without resistance, without challenge, without pain.

Hick acknowledged that this framework does not account for the worst cases, the suffering that is so extreme, so prolonged, or so pointless that it seems to crush rather than develop the soul. A child dying slowly of a degenerative disease is not being "built up" by the experience. The soul-making theodicy must not be turned into a sanctification of cruelty. It can account for the general structure of a world that includes suffering; it cannot account for every instance of suffering within that world. Hick himself ultimately appealed to eschatology, to the hope that in a life beyond this one, the process of soul-making will be completed and the suffering will be redeemed. This is a hope, not a proof. And it must be held as such.

## The Protest Tradition

One of the most neglected resources in the Christian response to suffering is the tradition of protest, the biblical tradition that does not answer the question of suffering but refuses to let it be silenced.

The book of Job is the foundational text. Job is a righteous man who suffers catastrophically, he loses his children, his health, his wealth, his standing. His friends arrive and offer theodicy: you must have sinned; God is disciplining you; there is a hidden purpose. Job rejects all of it. He demands an audience with God. He insists on his innocence. He accuses God of injustice. And the remarkable thing is that when God finally speaks, God does not answer Job's question. God answers out of the whirlwind with a cascade of questions about the foundations of the earth, the habits of the mountain goat, the behavior of the Leviathan, a speech that is, depending on your reading, either a profound assertion of divine mystery or a cosmic change of subject. But the most telling detail comes at the end: God rebukes not Job but his friends. The ones who offered tidy theodicy are the ones God condemns. The one who protested is the one God vindicates.

The lament psalms, Psalm 13, Psalm 22, Psalm 44, Psalm 88, institutionalize protest as a form of prayer. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" is not a failure of faith. It is a psalm. It is worship. It is the refusal to let go of God even in the experience of God's absence. Psalm 88 is the darkest text in the Psalter, it ends in darkness, with no resolution, no turn to praise, no note of hope. And the tradition preserved it. It included it in the hymnal. It said, in effect: this, too, is a legitimate way to speak to God.

Walter Brueggemann has described this tradition as "the costly loss of lament", the church's gradual abandonment of the lament tradition in favor of a relentlessly positive worship culture that has no room for darkness, complaint, or protest. The result, Brueggemann argues, is a theology that cannot bear the weight of reality. A God who can only be praised is a God too fragile for the world as it actually is.

## What Theodicy Cannot Do

Here is what must be said plainly, with no hedging: theodicy cannot explain a child's death to a parent. It cannot make a genocide intelligible. It cannot redeem the suffering of the Holocaust or the Middle Passage or the cancer ward by fitting it into a system. Any theodicy that claims to have "solved" the problem of evil has betrayed itself. The problem of evil is not a problem like a math problem, something with a solution that, once found, dissolves the difficulty. It is a problem like a wound. It does not want a solution. It wants a presence.

The danger of theodicy is that it can become a way of protecting God from the accusation of the sufferer, and in doing so, it becomes a way of silencing the sufferer. When a parent buries a child and a well-meaning Christian says, "God has a plan," the function of that statement is not to comfort the parent. The function is to comfort the speaker, to preserve their own theological framework from the threat that the parent's grief represents. It is, as Nicholas Wolterstorff wrote in *Lament for a Son* after the death of his own child, "a way of not looking at the suffering." The sufferer does not need an explanation. The sufferer needs someone willing to sit in the wreckage without explaining it away.

## The Cross as God's Answer

The Christian response to suffering is not, finally, a philosophical argument. It is a person nailed to a piece of wood.

The cross is not an explanation of suffering. It is God's entrance into suffering. The incarnation, the claim that God became a human being in Jesus of Nazareth, means that God is not a distant observer of human pain. God has been inside it. God has experienced abandonment, betrayal, torture, and death. The cry of dereliction from the cross, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?", is not a theological statement. It is a scream from the center of the abyss, uttered by the one who, Christians believe, is the Creator of the universe.

Jurgen Moltmann, in *The Crucified God* (1974), argued that the cross reveals a God who suffers, not a God who stands above suffering and permits it for mysterious purposes, but a God who enters into the deepest suffering and bears it from within. The cross does not answer the question "Why?" It answers the question "Where is God?" God is not in the observer's gallery. God is on the gallows. God is in the rubble. God is in the oncology ward at three in the morning when the morphine is not enough.

This does not make suffering acceptable. It does not make it purposeful. It does not resolve the philosophical problem. What it does, if it does anything, is reframe the question. The question is no longer "Why does God allow this?" The question becomes "What kind of God enters this?" And the Christian answer is: a God who would rather die than leave us alone in the darkness.

Dietrich Bonhoeffer, writing from a Nazi prison cell in 1944, put it this way: "Only the suffering God can help." Not the omnipotent God who could prevent suffering but chooses not to. Not the distant God who watches from above. The suffering God. The God who is with us in it, not above it. The God who does not explain the darkness but enters it and refuses to let it have the last word.

## What Remains

I do not have an answer to the problem of suffering. I have a response. The response is not a system but a set of convictions held in tension: that God is good, that the world is broken, that free will matters, that suffering can produce depth but is not justified by its products, that protest is a form of faith, that the cross means God is not a spectator, and that the resurrection means suffering is not the final word.

I hold all of these convictions while standing in a world where children die of cancer and earthquakes bury villages and the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer. I hold them not because they resolve the tension but because they are the most honest framework I have found for living inside the tension without either abandoning God or pretending the suffering is not real.

The parent who buries a child does not need my theodicy. They need my presence. They need the community of faith to sit with them in the ashes, to weep with them, to refuse to fill the silence with explanations that serve the explainer more than the bereaved. They need a faith tradition that has room for protest, for rage, for the unanswerable question hurled at heaven. They need a God who can absorb that question without flinching, who has, in fact, already absorbed it, on a cross, in the darkness, with a cry that shook the earth.

That is not an answer. It is the beginning of one. And it is all I have.

chapters.title: Why Would a Good God Allow So Much Evil?
chapters.summary: The suffering in the world is the oldest and heaviest reason to doubt God, and it deserves to be answered at full weight rather than waved away.
chapters.body:
This is the one that actually keeps people up at night. Not the clever objections, not the debates about miracles or morality, but the child with cancer, the village swallowed by the wave, the cruelty that lands on people who did nothing to deserve it. If God is all-powerful, He could stop it. If He is all-good, He would want to. It happens anyway, in oceans, every day. So either He cannot stop it, in which case He is not the God anyone means by the word, or He will not, in which case His goodness is a word that has lost its meaning. This is the problem of evil, and it is not a problem you solve. It is a wound you live with, and any answer that does not feel the wound is not an answer worth having.

Let me state it at its full and terrible strength, because the cheap versions of faith deserve to be broken against it. The argument is not improved by adding up the suffering, though the sheer quantity is staggering. It is sharpest at a single point. Take one child, one instance of innocent agony, the kind that does no one any good, that teaches no lesson, that simply destroys. The philosopher who pressed this hardest, building on Dostoevsky, said he would refuse a heaven built on the unavenged tears of one tortured child, would hand back the ticket. That is the objection at its most honest. It is not asking for a theory. It is holding up a single suffering face and asking how any good purpose could be worth that, and it is right to ask, and the believer who answers too quickly has not looked at the face.

So I am not going to offer you the small answers, because they fail in front of that face. The answer that suffering builds character fails, because some suffering destroys character, breaks people past repair, and because no decent person would torture a child to improve him. The answer that it is all part of a plan we cannot see fails as comfort, even if it is true in some sense, because it asks the grieving to be consoled by a blueprint they are not allowed to read. The answer that everyone gets what they deserve fails most of all, because Jesus Himself flatly rejected it, when they asked him whose sin caused a man's blindness and he said neither this man nor his parents, and when he refused to read the people crushed by a falling tower as worse sinners than anyone else. The Bible does not teach that suffering is distributed according to desert. The book of Job exists precisely to destroy that idea, and God's final word in Job is not an explanation. It is His own overwhelming presence, and a long refusal to give Job the theory he demanded. That refusal is itself a clue, and I will come back to it.

What the tradition does offer is not a single answer but a few true things that, taken together, change the shape of the question without dissolving the pain. The first is about freedom. A world with creatures who can genuinely love is a world with creatures who can genuinely refuse, and you cannot have the one without the other, because love that cannot be withheld is not love but a mechanism. A great deal of the world's evil, by far the most of it, is the cost of that freedom, the wars and cruelties and betrayals that are human choices and not divine ones. God could prevent every evil by removing every freedom, by reducing us to puppets who cannot harm because we cannot act, but the price would be the destruction of the very thing that makes us capable of love, and a universe of safe puppets may be a worse universe than this one. That does not cover the cancer or the wave, the suffering no one chose, and I am not pretending it does. But it covers more than people think, once you count honestly how much of the world's agony is delivered by one human hand to another.

The second true thing is harder and goes against the grain of how we frame the whole problem. The objection assumes that we are competent to judge, that if we cannot see a good reason for some suffering then there probably is none. But that assumption is doing enormous unnoticed work. To know that an instance of suffering serves no possible good purpose, you would have to see all of its consequences, down every branching path, across all of time, in every life it touches and every life those lives touch. No human being is in a position to make that judgment, and we know we are not, because we experience it constantly on a small scale. The pain that felt purely destructive at thirty turns out, at fifty, to have been the hinge everything good turned on, and we could not have seen it at the time. This does not mean all suffering has a hidden purpose we could endorse if we saw it. It means our inability to see a purpose is weak evidence that there is none, because our vantage point is so small. The argument from evil quietly requires us to be far more knowing than we are.

There is a third thing the tradition says, and it is the one most easily turned into a cruelty, so I will handle it carefully. Christianity claims that something went wrong with the world, that it is not now as it was made to be, that a rupture runs through the whole of creation and not only through human choices. This is not the claim that each sufferer deserves his suffering, which Jesus flatly denied. It is the larger claim that we live in a wounded world, a creation that the Bible describes as groaning, subjected to decay, waiting to be set right. On this view the cancer and the wave are not God's verdicts on particular people. They are symptoms of a deep disorder in the fabric of things, a brokenness that touches everything and falls, like rain, on the just and the unjust alike. This does not tell you why your child and not another, and I will not pretend it does. But it refuses the two cruelties that usually fill the silence, the cruelty of saying you must have deserved it and the cruelty of saying this is exactly how a good world should run. It says neither. It says the world is broken, that God knows it, and that He has not left it broken.

But I promised not to hide behind theory, and these two points, true as they are, remain theory, and theory does not weep. So let me tell you what is actually different about the Christian answer, because in the end it is not an argument at all. Every other system, when confronted with this, tries to explain suffering, to fit it into a scheme that makes it acceptable, to get God off the hook by giving you a reason. Christianity does something stranger and, I think, far more to the point. It does not finally explain suffering. It says that God entered it.

This is the center, and it is the thing the world's other answers do not have. The God of the Christians is not a distant being who arranged a world of pain and watches it from a place where pain cannot reach Him, handing down explanations from the safe seats. He came down into it. He took on a body that could be tortured and was. He was betrayed by a friend, abandoned by the rest, beaten, mocked, and nailed to a post to suffocate in public, and at the worst of it He cried out that even God had forsaken Him. Whatever you think happened on that cross, you cannot say that the Christian God does not know what suffering is from the inside. He is not the absent landlord of a burning house. He walked into the fire. The deepest answer Christianity gives to the problem of evil is not a sentence. It is a wounded man on a cross, and the claim that the man is God.

Why does this matter, if it does not stop the suffering. It matters because the real anguish of the problem of evil is not finally intellectual. It is the fear that the suffering means we are alone, that the universe is indifferent, that no one sees and no one cares and there is no one to cry to. The cross does not answer the question why. It answers the deeper question, the one underneath, which is whether we are alone in it. And the Christian answer is no. God is not the cause of your suffering held at a distance. He is the one who has joined you in it, who has been to the bottom of the worst of it before you, who meets you there not with a lecture but with His own scars. Dostoevsky's challenge, the unavenged tears of the child, gets its real answer not in a theory but in a person who took the tears of the world into Himself and answered them with His own blood.

And there is the second half, without which the cross is only a tragedy. Christianity does not end at the suffering. It claims that the suffering was not the last word, that the tortured man walked out of the grave, and that this is the preview of what God intends for the whole groaning world. The promise is not that the suffering had a tidy purpose. The promise is that it will be undone, that there is coming a day when, as the old text says, He will wipe away every tear, when death itself dies, when the wave and the cancer and the cruelty are not merely explained but defeated and reversed. The Christian hope is not that the child's suffering will be justified by some greater good in the ledger. It is that the child will be raised, healed, made whole, and that the God who wept will set it right in a way that does not balance the books but breaks them, swallowing the evil in a flood of restored life. That is either true or it is not, and everything hangs on whether the tomb was empty. But if it is true, then the tears are not the end of the child's story, and the One who refuses, with Dostoevsky, to accept a heaven built on unavenged tears, turns out to agree with God, who did not accept it either, and did something about it at infinite cost to Himself.

So I will not close this neatly, because the wound is still open and will be until that day. You will still stand at gravesides. The wave will still come. I have buried children and I have no formula that makes that bearable, and I distrust anyone who says he does. What I have, what the faith offers, is not an explanation that makes the suffering acceptable. It is a God who came into it, who suffered it Himself, who promises to end it, and who asks you, in the meantime, not to understand but to trust, the way Job finally trusted, not because he got his answer but because he met the One who was big enough to be trusted with the question. The problem of evil is the strongest case against God. It is also, in the strangest turn, the place where the Christian God comes closest, because He is the only God who has the wounds to show you. Whether that is enough is something you will have to decide standing where the suffering actually is, which is the only place the question was ever really asked.
